enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low risk / Not applicable (cross-sectional census of 1,189 US utilities serving >=40,000 residents; only 6 observations missing from regression models, N = 1,183, including 2 dropped in Alaska and Hawaii due to unavailable NOAA PDSI climate division data).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Moderate-to-high concern (cross-sectional OLS controls for log population, log median income, 10-year PDSI water scarcity, groundwater/purchased source water, % Hispanic, and % Black, but omits established local political and institutional confounders such as citizen political ideology, special-district vs. municipal governance structure, and state fixed effects; R-squared is 0.062 and authors note unobserved political factors may correlate with both inequality and rate structures).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate with minor classification limitations (public vs. investor-owned governance status is drawn from federal EPA SDWIS records and residential rate schedules are collected directly from 2019 utility tariffs, but Endnote 3 notes that state PUCs in Indiana, Maine, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin also regulate some or all government-owned utilities, blurring the binary local-electoral vs. state-PUC institutional distinction; municipal service areas are approximated by city limits).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some concern (residential tariff schedules and EPA SDWIS records are objective, but community income inequality from 2017 ACS 5-year estimates involves sampling error and GIS tract-to-service-area areal/population weighting or municipal city-limit approximations, and household-level water billing/income microdata are unavailable).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for rate-schedule progressivity, limited for realized household redistribution (the Unit Price Ratio comparing average unit prices at 12,000-60,000 gal/month to a 6,000 gal/month baseline is transparently and consistently computed from official 2019 single-family tariffs, but excludes sewer charges, low-income assistance programs, and actual household consumption by income tier).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern / No pre-registration (no pre-analysis plan is reported; full results and p-values are transparently reported in Table 4 and text, including the statistically non-significant Private x Inequality interaction p = 0.387, although the Abstract and Introduction overstate public-private divergence by emphasizing separate subsample null results rather than the non-significant interaction test).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Low concern within target population, limited generalizability to small systems (complete census sampling frame from EPA SDWIS of all 1,189 US community water systems serving >=40,000 residents, covering ~58% of US water customers, with 99.5% completeness in regressions, N = 1,183; excludes smaller utilities serving <40,000 people).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion criteria are explicitly defined using the US EPA Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) as every community water system in the United States serving a population of at least 40,000 residents (1,189 utilities total; 2 utilities in Alaska and Hawaii excluded from regression due to missing NOAA PDSI data, yielding N = 1,183).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 9-10, 13, 19 (Research Design: Data; Sampling and data collection, pp. 373-374; Table 3, p. 377; Endnote 13, p. 383)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The institutional and regulatory setting of US drinking water utilities (local government legislative rate-setting vs. state Public Utilities Commission quasi-judicial rate-setting for investor-owned utilities) and sample characteristics (1,055 local government and 134 investor-owned utilities serving 183.3 million residents across 218 climate divisions, with full descriptive statistics in Tables 1 and 3) are thoroughly described.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 3-5, 10, 13 (Water Utility Service and Pricing in the United States, pp. 367-369; Sampling and data collection, p. 374; Table 1, p. 374; Table 3, p. 377)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Income inequality is operationalized via the mean-to-median household income ratio from 2017 US Census ACS 5-year estimates (cross-checked against the Gini coefficient, r = 0.92, with substantively similar results) and utility ownership is taken from EPA SDWIS. Minor measurement error arises from ACS sampling error, approximating municipal utility boundaries with city limits vs. tract-weighted GIS boundaries elsewhere, and not separating the four states where PUCs also regulate public utilities (Endnote 3).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 12, 18-19 (Income inequality and other covariates, p. 376; Endnotes 3, 10-12, pp. 382-383)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Community water system classification, population threshold (>=40,000), and public vs. private ownership are determined from standardized federal regulatory records in EPA SDWIS, and residential rate structures are coded directly from official utility tariff schedules.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 10, 12, 18 (Sampling and data collection, p. 374; Income inequality and other covariates, p. 376; Endnote 6, p. 382)

domain_ratings.justification: The authors identify key fiscal, hydrological, source-water, and demographic confounders (utility size, median household income, 10-year PDSI drought scarcity, groundwater reliance, purchased wholesale water, % Hispanic, and % Black) and acknowledge in the Limitations section that unobserved political factors could correlate with both inequality and rate progressivity, though previously cited institutional/political predictors (e.g., local voter ideology, special district vs. general-purpose municipal governance, state regulatory regimes) are omitted from the models.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 7, 12-13, 17 (Political economy of water pricing, p. 371; Income inequality and other covariates, pp. 376-377; Limitations and directions for future research, p. 381)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: The study employs multivariable OLS regression controlling for demographic, fiscal, hydrological, and water-source covariates alongside an ownership interaction test (private investor-owned utilities as an institutional counterfactual). However, the purely cross-sectional design lacks state fixed effects and omits local political ideology and municipal vs. special-district governance controls, leaving substantial residual confounding risk (R-squared = 0.062).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 9, 12-14, 17 (Inequality and public enterprise pricing, p. 373; Income inequality and other covariates & Estimation and results, pp. 376-378; Table 4, p. 378; Limitations, p. 381)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Residential water price progressivity is objectively calculated from published Jan-Apr 2019 single-family tariff schedules (plus email/phone follow-up for 5 utilities) using the Unit Price Ratio (UPR) comparing average unit cost (fixed plus volumetric) at 12,000-60,000 gal/month against the literature-standard 6,000 gal/month basic indoor need benchmark. While valid as a tariff-structure metric, it does not capture customer-level water consumption by income, low-income bill assistance, or wastewater charges.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 10-11, 18 (Measuring price progressivity, pp. 374-375; Table 2, p. 375; Endnotes 5-6, p. 382)

domain_ratings.justification: Multivariable OLS with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and sensitivity checks across volume thresholds (12,000-60,000 gal/month) and alternative inequality metrics (Gini) are appropriate for cross-sectional continuous UPR analysis, though standard errors are not clustered by state/PUC and the Private x Inequality interaction in Model B is statistically non-significant (b = -0.209, p = 0.387), meaning the data do not statistically confirm a difference in slopes between public and private utilities despite strong subsample claims in the Abstract.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1, 13-16, 19 (Abstract, p. 365; Estimation and results, p. 377; Table 4, p. 378; Results, pp. 378-380; Endnote 17, p. 383)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Switzer and Teodoro (2025) present a well-documented analytical cross-sectional regression study of nearly the entire universe of large US community water systems serving >=40,000 residents (1,189 utilities; N = 1,183 analyzed), testing whether local income inequality predicts residential water rate progressivity (Unit Price Ratio at 12,000-60,000 vs. 6,000 gal/month) and whether this relationship differs between local government utilities and PUC-regulated investor-owned utilities. Strengths include census coverage of large US systems via EPA SDWIS, direct collection of 2019 single-family tariff schedules with minimal missingness, robustness checks across consumption thresholds and Gini inequality, and candid discussion of limitations. Overall methodological concern is rated 'Some concern' under the JBI Analytical Cross Sectional Checklist because: (1) the cross-sectional OLS design cannot rule out unobserved political/institutional confounders—notably local citizen political ideology, special-district versus municipal governance form, and state-level regulatory fixed effects (model R-squared = 0.062); (2) institutional classification treats all government-owned utilities uniformly even though state PUCs regulate public utilities in four states (Endnote 3) and municipal service areas are approximated by city limits; (3) outcome progressivity is measured from rate schedules at fixed benchmark volumes rather than customer-level billing and income microdata; and (4) the key Private x Inequality interaction term in Model B is not statistically significant (p = 0.387), tempering claims of differential responsiveness between public and investor-owned utilities.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Observational analytical cross-sectional regression study of 1,189 US community water utilities serving >=40,000 residents (N = 1,183 analyzed via OLS)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research Design, Sampling and Data Collection, Measurement, Estimation, and Results on PDF pp. 9-16 (journal pp. 373-380); Institutional background on PDF pp. 3-7 (pp. 367-371); Limitations on PDF p. 17 (p. 381); Endnotes 1-17 on PDF pp. 18-19 (pp. 382-383).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical component is a single-wave cross-sectional OLS regression linking 2017 Census ACS community income inequality and EPA SDWIS utility ownership to Jan-Apr 2019 residential water rate progressivity across 1,183 US utilities, with no longitudinal panel, policy intervention shock, or quasi-experimental design (ruling out ROBINS-I), and only brief secondary literature/news vignettes on pp. 370-371 rather than primary qualitative data collection (ruling out MMAT). Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact design-matched tool.
